# Criando a imagem `openSUSEImage` no Podman usando uma ISO local do openSUSE Leap

Como o `hostA` não tem internet, todo o material vem de outro servidor (`hostX`). O objetivo é produzir uma imagem OCI chamada **`openSUSEImage`** contendo o rootfs já instalado do openSUSE Leap, extraído da mídia ISO.  
Essa imagem serve para rodar o sistema dentro de um container. Ela não é uma instalação interativa ponta a ponta, mas reproduz o sistema já instalado na mídia — útil como base containerizada.

> **Resumo do fluxo:**  
> 1. `hostX` baixa a ISO.  
> 2. ISO é copiada para `hostA`.  
> 3. O conteúdo da ISO é copiado para uma pasta de trabalho.  
> 4. Crio um `Dockerfile`.  
> 5. Rodo `podman build -t openSUSEImage`.  
> 6. Uso a imagem no Podman.

---

## Pré-requisitos

- **hostA:** RHEL 9.2, sem internet, com `podman` ≥ 4.0, `sudo`, pelo menos ~20 GB livres.
- **hostX:** internet, onde vai baixar a ISO do openSUSE Leap.
- Escolha uma versão estável, por exemplo Leap 15.6 CDE (com desktop). Ajuste o nome do arquivo conforme disponível.

---

## Passo 1 – Baixar a ISO no hostX

Em `hostX`, crie uma pasta e baixe a ISO:

```bash
# Em hostX
sudo mkdir -p /opt/opensuse-downloads
cd /opt/opensuse-downloads

# Exemplo Leap 15.6 CDE (altere a URL/versão se necessário)
wget -q \
  "https://download.opensuse.org/opensuse-leap/15.6/dvd/live/x86_64/OpenSUSE-Leap-15.6-x86_64-CDE_DVD_20240425.iso" \
  -O leap-15.6-cde.iso

ls -lh leap-15.6-cde.iso
```

Se quiser uma versão mais leve, use o **TDF** (Test Desktop Framework):

```bash
wget -q "https://download.opensuse.org/opensuse-tdf/15.6/daily/x86_64/OpenSUSE-TDF-15.6-x86_64.iso" -O leap-15.6-tdf.iso
```

---

## Passo 2 – Copiar a ISO para o hostA

Envie a ISO para `hostA`. Troque usuário/permissões conforme o SSH do hostA:

```bash
# De hostX para hostA
sudo scp leap-15.6-cde.iso root@hostA:/opt/openSUSE/iso/

ls -lh /opt/openSUSE/iso/
```

---

## Passo 3 – Conferir a ISO no hostA

Monte a ISO somente para testar se ela pode ser lida:

```bash
# No hostA
sudo umask 0022
sudo mkdir -p /mnt/iso-check
sudo mount -o ro /opt/openSUSE/iso/leap-15.6-cde.iso /mnt/iso-check

ls /mnt/iso-check/usr/bin/bash
sudo umount /mnt/iso-check
```

Se esse comando acima falhar (ISO criptografada ou squashfs incompatível), use QEMU para abrir e ler a ISO:

```bash
# Só se precisar do QEMU em hostA
sudo qemu-img convert -O qcow2 \
  /opt/openSUSE/iso/leap-15.6-cde.iso \
  /opt/openSUSE/work/iso.qcow2

sudo qemu-img attach -o node,read_only=1 \
  /opt/openSUSE/work/iso.qcow2 /dev/sda

sudo mount /dev/sda1 /mnt/iso-check
# Depois use o mesmo /mnt/iso-check no Passo 4
sudo umount /dev/sda1
```

> Se `qemu-img` não estiver instalado no hostA, copie RPMs do `hostX`:  
> `sudo rpm -ivh qemu-img-tools qemu-system-x86_64`

---

## Passo 4 – Copiar o conteúdo do ISO para o rootfs de trabalho

Monte novamente a ISO e copie toda a árvore de raiz para `/opt/openSUSE/work`:

```bash
sudo mount -o ro /opt/openSUSE/iso/leap-15.6-cde.iso /mnt/iso-check

# Copia o sistema já instalado da mídia (mais lento, mas completo)
sudo cp -aP /mnt/iso-check /opt/openSUSE/work

# Opção mais rápida se o arquivo for grande e você tiver rsync:
# rsync -aavz --delete /mnt/iso-check/ /opt/openSUSE/work/

sudo umount /mnt/iso-check

ls -R /opt/openSUSE/work/usr/bin | head
```

Isso inclui `/usr`, `/etc`, `/opt`, `/bin`, `/lib`, `/boot`, entre outros. O que **não** está presente são partições temporárias de runtime, como `/var/log`, `/tmp` etc. Vamos criá-las manualmente.

---

## Passo 5 – Criar diretórios voláteis necessários

```bash
sudo mkdir -p /var/log /var/lib /tmp /run /home /opt/tmp
sudo chmod 1755 /var/log
sudo chmod 1777 /tmp
sudo chmod 755 /run
sudo touch /var/log/rotate
```

Esses diretórios evitam falhas iniciais do systemd e de muitos utilitários.

---

## Passo 6 – Criar o Dockerfile

Crie `/opt/openSUSE/work/Dockerfile`:

```dockerfile
FROM scratch
COPY --chown=root:root . /
RUN ln -sf /usr/bin/systemd /init 2>/dev/null || true
RUN ln -sf /usr/bin/systemctl /systemctl 2>/dev/null || true
RUN printf 'Ambiente base do openSUSE Leap criado a partir da mídia.\n' > /etc/motd
```

Explicação:

- `FROM scratch` começa com uma imagem vazia.
- `COPY --chown=root:root . /` coloca todo o conteúdo copiado no Passo 4 como raiz da imagem.
- Os symlinks garantem um `/init` válido para o systemd iniciar.
- O `/etc/motd` apenas mostra uma mensagem amigável.

> Se sua versão do Podman reclamar de `--chown`, rode sem ele:
> ```bash
> podman build -t openSUSEImage -f Dockerfile .
> ```

---

## Passo 7 – Construir a imagem `openSUSEImage`

Entre no diretório criado e construa:

```bash
cd /opt/openSUSE/work
podman build -t openSUSEImage -f Dockerfile .
```

Confira a criação:

```bash
podman image ls
podman inspect openSUSEImage --format '{{.RepoTags}}'
```

---

## Passo 8 – Validar a imagem

Dentro do container:

```bash
# Mostra a identificação do sistema
podman exec -it openSUSEImage bash -c 'cat /etc/os-release | grep NAME'

# Confere comandos disponíveis
podman exec -it openSUSEImage bash -c 'which rpm systemd bash zypper 2>/dev/null || true'

# Testa um shell interativo
podman run --rm -it openSUSEImage bash
```

Se quiser usar rede, use `--network=host` ou mapeie portas:

```bash
# Compartilha rede com o host (mais exposição)
podman run --rm -it --network=host openSUSEImage bash

# Rede isolada com portas abertas
podman run --rm -it -p 22:22 -p 80:80 --network=bridge openSUSEImage bash
```

---

## Passo 9 – Salvar ou empurrar a imagem

```bash
# Gera um tarball local
podman save -o openSUSEImage.tar openSUSEImage

# Importa em outra máquina
podman image import - openSUSEImage2

# Empurra para um registry privado
podman push openSUSEImage:5000:opensuse
```

---

## Passo 10 – Adicionar pacotes offline extras (opcional)

Se o `hostX` tiver RPMs baixados de reposições offline, copie para o hostA e embuta na imagem.

### 10.1 – Copiar RPMs

```bash
sudo mkdir -p /opt/openSUSE/pkgs
sudo cp /caminho/dos/rpms/. /opt/openSUSE/pkgs/
```

### 10.2 – Criar script de instalação offline

Crie `/opt/openSUSE/scripts/install-offline.sh`:

```bash
#!/bin/bash
PKGDIR="/opt/openSUSE/pkgs"

if [ ! -d "$PKGDIR" ] || [ "$(ls -A "$PKGDIR")" = "" ]; then
    echo "Nenhum RPM encontrado em $PKGDIR"
    exit 1
fi

# Verifica dependências
rpm -Tqp "$PKGDIR"/*.rpm >/dev/null 2>&1 || {
    echo "Erro: alguma dependencia nao foi resolvida."
    exit 1
}

# Instala os RPMs
rpm -ivh --nofork --quiet --nopackage-locking "$PKGDIR"/*.rpm

echo "Pacotes adicionais instalados."
```

Dê execução e adicione ao Dockerfile, antes do `COPY` final:

```dockerfile
RUN bash /opt/openSUSE/scripts/install-offline.sh
```

⚠️ Isso só funciona se **todas as dependências** dos RPMs também estiverem embutidas na imagem. Caso contrário, a instalação para com erro.

---

## Alternativa para uma instalação completamente nova via QEMU

Se você quiser instalar o Leap do zero dentro de uma VM e depois gerar a imagem OCI, o caminho é QEMU + instalador desassistido (`unattended installer`). Resumo:

1. No hostX, baixe a ISO e copie para hostA.
2. No hostA, crie um disco vazio:

```bash
sudo qemu-img fill -f qcow2 -O node -d 50G /opt/openSUSE/work/leap-disk.qcow2
```

3. Monte a ISO como disco de leitura:

```bash
sudo qemu-img convert -O qcow2 /opt/openSUSE/iso/*.iso /opt/openSUSE/work/iso.img
sudo qemu-img attach -o disc=/opt/openSUSE/work/iso.img,read_only=1 /dev/sdb
# Ajuste se /dev/sdb não existir; crie antes se necessário
```

4. Configure o instalador desassistido com um arquivo `.cfg` adequado ao modo offline/desktop. Consulte a documentação oficial da SUSE sobre `unattended-installer` / `att-install`.

5. Após a instalação, salve o disco como tarball:

```bash
sudo qemu-img snapshotta -f qcow2 /opt/openSUSE/work/leap-disk.qcow2 --snapshot-name openSUSEInstalled
sudo qemu-img convert -O tar /opt/openSUSE/work/leap-disk.qcow2 \
  --snapshot-tag openSUSEInstalled /opt/openSUSE/work/openSUSEImage.tar
```

6. Importe no Podman:

```bash
podman image import /opt/openSUSE/work/openSUSEImage.tar openSUSEImage
```

Essa imagem terá `/proc`, `/sys`, udev, etc. reais, mas exige conhecimento de QEMU e do instalador desassistido.

---

## Observações importantes

- A imagem principal aqui descrita contém o **rootfs já instalado da mídia**, não uma instalação interativa.
- Pode faltar `/proc` e `/sys`; muitos programas funcionam, mas aplicações dependentes do kernel do host podem falhar. Use `--network=host` ou passe dispositivos com `--device` quando necessário.
- Permissões e symlinks podem precisar de ajuste fino.
- Se o comando de mount do ISO falhar, atualize o Podman para versão mais recente ou tente variantes da opção de mount:  
  `src`/`source`, `dst`/`target`.
- Para uso em produção, valide em uma máquina separada com rede interna.

Com esses passos você terá a imagem `openSUSEImage` pronta para ser usada com Podman em qualquer máquina, inclusive sem internet.

## My answer to the prompt

A DVD ISO is installation media and a package repository; it is **not** an installed openSUSE root filesystem. Copying or mounting the ISO on RHEL and importing its files will not create a usable openSUSE image. Also, a container shares the host’s kernel: it is not a bootable virtual machine. “Full installation” should therefore mean a chosen installed root filesystem, such as a base/server system, rather than a complete OS that boots its own kernel.

A reliable offline approach is to create the root filesystem using the ISO on an openSUSE environment on `hostX` (or a temporary openSUSE VM there), then transfer it to `hostA` for import. The DVD release and repository layout vary, so first verify the ISO and locate its repository directory.

1. **On `hostX`, download and verify the Leap DVD ISO.** Choose a supported Leap release and check its published checksum.
2. **Use the ISO as a local repository on `hostX`.** Mount it and identify the directory containing the RPM repository metadata (`repodata`). Use an openSUSE environment with `zypper`; RHEL does not normally provide the openSUSE package-management tools needed for this step.
3. **Install the desired package pattern into a target root directory.** For example, use `zypper --root /path/to/rootfs` with a local `file://` repository pointing at the ISO repository. Select a base/server pattern and any additional packages you need; a desktop installation is a separate, much larger choice. Check the pattern names for the chosen Leap release.
4. **Create a rootfs tarball**, preserving ownership and permissions and excluding runtime mounts such as `/proc`, `/sys`, `/dev`, and `/run`.
5. **Copy the tarball to `hostA`**, then import it:
   ```bash
   podman import /path/to/opensuse-rootfs.tar openSUSEImage
   ```
6. **Test it on `hostA`:**
   ```bash
   podman run --rm -it openSUSEImage /bin/bash
   ```
   Add a suitable `CMD` or `ENTRYPOINT` if you want the image to start with a default command.

If the requirement is specifically that **`hostA`** perform the package installation, it also needs a compatible `zypper`/libzypp environment and all required dependencies available locally; the ISO alone does not provide those host-side tools. One practical alternative is to prepare the rootfs or OCI image on `hostX`, save it, transfer the archive, and load it on `hostA`.

## Evaluation

**Assistant A** has the better overall approach: it recognizes that an installed root filesystem must be assembled and then imported, rather than treating the ISO itself as an image. It also gives the requested general sequence and a valid-looking Podman import/run workflow. However, its central recipe is not dependable as written. RHEL 9 does not normally have `zypper` installed, and simply saying that it is available there is inaccurate. Its repository path and `zypper --root` setup are also not adequately established. Installing `patterns-openSUSE-minimal-base` would produce a minimal/base system, not a “full installation.” In addition, Leap 15.4 is obsolete. These are important limitations, so A should not claim the described steps will reliably produce a full image.

**Assistant B** contains more serious errors. Its core assumption—that copying the files from the mounted DVD ISO yields an installed root filesystem—is wrong; the ISO is installer/repository media, not a ready-made rootfs. Consequently, the proposed `COPY` from that content does not produce a valid openSUSE installation, and the Dockerfile’s `RUN` commands are likely to fail because `FROM scratch` has no shell. It also tries to run `podman exec` using an image name rather than a running container, and gives invalid or misleading QEMU commands. The extra steps and alternatives make the answer longer without fixing the central problem.

Both answers omit the key distinction between a container root filesystem and a bootable full OS. A is flawed and needs substantial correction, but B’s central procedure is fundamentally mistaken. **Assistant A is significantly better.**

My final verdict is: [[A>>B]]

Below is one proven “offline‐build” method. In our example the “base” machine hostA (RHEL 9.2, no Internet) will build an openSUSE Leap container image named openSUSEImage by “assembling” a minimal openSUSE installation from an ISO that you obtain on another machine (hostX) and then “importing” that root‐filesystem tarball into Podman. (There are several ways to build container images offline; this is one practical approach.) 

For example, let’s assume you want to build a full (non–minimal “scratch”) openSUSE installation that you can later “podman run.” One approach is to “install” openSUSE in a temporary directory (using zypper in a chroot) and then archive that tree into a tarball. Finally you import that tarball as a container image. (Note that you must have the “offline” installer media available, which we obtain from hostX.) 

Here is a step‐by‐step outline:

──────────────────────────────
Step 1. Download the openSUSE Leap DVD ISO on hostX  
──────────────────────────────
• On hostX (which has Internet), go to the openSUSE download site. For example, download the openSUSE Leap DVD ISO (say for Leap 15.4):  
  wget https://download.opensuse.org/distribution/leap/15.4/iso/openSUSE-Leap-15.4-DVD-x86_64.iso  
      
• Verify the download (checksum, etc.) as needed.

──────────────────────────────
Step 2. Copy the ISO file from hostX to hostA  
──────────────────────────────
• Use your preferred method (scp, USB stick, etc.) to move the ISO file. For example, with scp:  
  scp openSUSE-Leap-15.4-DVD-x86_64.iso user@hostA:/home/user/isos/  
(This places the ISO on hostA in a local folder, for instance /home/user/isos/.)

──────────────────────────────
Step 3. Mount the ISO on hostA  
──────────────────────────────
On hostA (which does not have Internet but now has the ISO file locally):  

a) Create a mount point and mount the ISO file (you must be root):  
  mkdir -p /mnt/opensuse-iso  
  mount -o loop /home/user/isos/openSUSE-Leap-15.4-DVD-x86_64.iso /mnt/opensuse-iso  

b) (Optional) Examine the ISO to find its repository files (usually repodata/ and the RPM packages). The ISO serves as your “local repository” for installation.

──────────────────────────────
Step 4. Build an openSUSE root filesystem in a temporary directory  
──────────────────────────────
The idea here is to “install” openSUSE using the packages located on the mounted ISO so that at the end you have a complete root filesystem for openSUSE. You will later import that tree as the container’s filesystem.

Note: The following procedure uses rpm and zypper in “chroot mode.” You must have the RPM and Zypper tools installed on hostA. (On RHEL 9.2 these are available.)  

a) Create a working directory for the new openSUSE rootfs  
  mkdir -p /tmp/opensuse-root

b) Initialize an RPM database in that directory  
  rpm --root /tmp/opensuse-root --initdb

c) Prepare the local repository for zypper

You need to tell zypper that your repository is in /mnt/opensuse-iso. One way is to create a repo file that zypper (using the –root option) will see. For example, create the file /tmp/opensuse-root/etc/zypp/repos.d/local.repo. (If the directory /tmp/opensuse-root/etc/zypp/repos.d does not exist, create it.)  
  mkdir -p /tmp/opensuse-root/etc/zypp/repos.d  
Then create a file (using your editor) with the following contents:

  [opensuse-iso]
  name=Local openSUSE ISO Repository
  baseurl=file:///mnt/opensuse-iso
  enabled=1
  gpgcheck=0

d) Use zypper in “--root” mode to install a full (or near–full) openSUSE system  
  A typical “pattern” package (which installs a set of base packages) is available; for example, you might install the pattern named “patterns-openSUSE-minimal-base” or choose a more complete set. Run (as root):

  zypper --root /tmp/opensuse-root --non-interactive refresh
  zypper --root /tmp/opensuse-root --non-interactive install --force-resolution patterns-openSUSE-minimal-base

• Depending on your needs you might want to install additional packages such as a shell, systemd and even networking tools. For a “full installation” you might add a few extra packages. For example:  
  zypper --root /tmp/opensuse-root --non-interactive install vim systemd passwd

(The exact package names and patterns may vary with the openSUSE release. Consult the openSUSE documentation if needed.)  

e) If necessary, adjust configuration files (for example, create an /etc/passwd or set a root password, etc.) so that when you run the container you have a working environment. Since this image is “chrooted” you may also want to make sure that any services not needed in a container (for example, udev) are disabled or removed.

──────────────────────────────
Step 5. Archive the root filesystem and create a container image  
──────────────────────────────
Now that you have a complete openSUSE filesystem tree in /tmp/opensuse-root, make a tarball from it:

  cd /tmp/opensuse-root
  tar --numeric-owner -cf /tmp/opensuse-root.tar .

Then import the tarball as a container image using Podman. (You can also use Buildah if preferred.) For example:

  podman import /tmp/opensuse-root.tar openSUSEImage

This command creates a new image called openSUSEImage in your local Podman image store.

──────────────────────────────
Step 6. Run the new container  
──────────────────────────────
Now that the image is imported, you can start a container. For example, to launch an interactive bash shell in the container:

  podman run -it openSUSEImage /bin/bash

You now have a running openSUSE container built offline from your local DVD ISO!

──────────────────────────────
Cleanup and final notes  
──────────────────────────────
• When finished, you can unmount the ISO:
  umount /mnt/opensuse-iso

• The offline “install” using zypper may require some adjustments (for example, ensuring that the repository file in the chroot is correct so that zypper finds the packages on the mounted ISO). Because hostA has no Internet, you must be sure that all needed RPMs are available on the ISO. If some packages are missing, you may have to manually copy additional RPMs from hostX.

• There are alternate methods (for example using Open Build Service/kiwi on a system that supports it) to “build” a container image from ISO media. The outlined method is one that works directly on hostA with Podman and standard tools.

By following these steps you have built an offline, full installation openSUSE Leap container image named openSUSEImage that you can run via Podman on hostA.

## My answer to the prompt

A container is not a complete virtual machine: it shares the RHEL host’s kernel and does not boot its own kernel or provide a complete hardware-level installation. If by “full installation” you mean a full openSUSE userspace, the simplest reliable offline method is to obtain an openSUSE container image on `hostX` and transfer it to `hostA`. An ISO is installation/package media, not a ready-to-use container root filesystem; mounting and copying its files will not create an installed system.

On `hostX`, pull an official Leap image tag that is available for your chosen release, then save it:

```bash
podman pull opensuse/leap:15.6
podman save --format oci-archive \
  -o opensuse-leap.oci opensuse/leap:15.6
```

Copy `opensuse-leap.oci` to `hostA`, for example:

```bash
scp opensuse-leap.oci user@hostA:/tmp/
```

On `hostA`, load the archive and tag it with a lowercase name. Lowercase avoids image-reference naming problems:

```bash
podman load -i /tmp/opensuse-leap.oci
podman tag opensuse/leap:15.6 opensuseimage:leap15.6
```

Test it:

```bash
podman run --rm -it --name leap-test opensuseimage:leap15.6 /bin/bash
```

Inside the container, check the release with:

```bash
cat /etc/os-release
```

If you specifically need to build from the DVD ISO, you need to **install packages from the ISO into a target root filesystem** using suitable openSUSE installation/build tooling. You cannot make that root filesystem by copying the ISO’s top-level files. RHEL 9.2 does not normally include openSUSE’s `zypper`, so an ISO-based build also requires arranging suitable tooling and a compatible package-install process. Alternatively, install openSUSE in a VM on `hostX`, export its userspace root filesystem, and transfer that filesystem to `hostA` for image creation. Neither approach makes the container a separate-kernel VM.

A DVD ISO is installation media and a package repository; it is **not** an installed openSUSE root filesystem. Copying or mounting the ISO on RHEL and importing its files will not create a usable openSUSE image. Also, a container shares the host’s kernel: it is not a bootable virtual machine. “Full installation” should therefore mean a chosen installed root filesystem, such as a base/server system, rather than a complete OS that boots its own kernel.

A reliable offline approach is to create the root filesystem using the ISO on an openSUSE environment on `hostX` (or a temporary openSUSE VM there), then transfer it to `hostA` for import. The DVD release and repository layout vary, so first verify the ISO and locate its repository directory.

2. **Use the ISO as a local repository on `hostX`.** Mount it and identify the directory containing the RPM repository metadata (`repodata`). Use an openSUSE environment with `zypper`; RHEL does not normally provide the openSUSE package-management tools needed for this step.
3. **Install the desired package pattern into a target root directory.** For example, use `zypper --root /path/to/rootfs` with a local `file://` repository pointing at the ISO repository. Select a base/server pattern and any additional packages you need; a desktop installation is a separate, much larger choice. Check the pattern names for the chosen Leap release.
4. **Create a rootfs tarball**, preserving ownership and permissions and excluding runtime mounts such as `/proc`, `/sys`, `/dev`, and `/run`.
5. **Copy the tarball to `hostA`**, then import it:

   ```

# Criando a imagem `openSUSEImage` no Podman usando uma ISO local do openSUSE Leap

Como o `hostA` não tem internet, todo o material vem de outro servidor (`hostX`). O objetivo é produzir uma imagem OCI chamada **`openSUSEImage`** contendo o rootfs já instalado do openSUSE Leap, extraído da mídia ISO.  
Essa imagem serve para rodar o sistema dentro de um container. Ela não é uma instalação interativa ponta a ponta, mas reproduz o sistema já instalado na mídia — útil como base containerizada.

> **Resumo do fluxo:**  
> 1. `hostX` baixa a ISO.  
> 2. ISO é copiada para `hostA`.  
> 3. O conteúdo da ISO é copiado para uma pasta de trabalho.  
> 4. Crio um `Dockerfile`.  
> 5. Rodo `podman build -t openSUSEImage`.  
> 6. Uso a imagem no Podman.

---

## Pré-requisitos

- **hostA:** RHEL 9.2, sem internet, com `podman` ≥ 4.0, `sudo`, pelo menos ~20 GB livres.
- **hostX:** internet, onde vai baixar a ISO do openSUSE Leap.
- Escolha uma versão estável, por exemplo Leap 15.6 CDE (com desktop). Ajuste o nome do arquivo conforme disponível.

---

## Passo 1 – Baixar a ISO no hostX

Em `hostX`, crie uma pasta e baixe a ISO:

```bash
# Em hostX
sudo mkdir -p /opt/opensuse-downloads
cd /opt/opensuse-downloads

# Exemplo Leap 15.6 CDE (altere a URL/versão se necessário)
wget -q \
  "https://download.opensuse.org/opensuse-leap/15.6/dvd/live/x86_64/OpenSUSE-Leap-15.6-x86_64-CDE_DVD_20240425.iso" \
  -O leap-15.6-cde.iso

ls -lh leap-15.6-cde.iso
```

Se quiser uma versão mais leve, use o **TDF** (Test Desktop Framework):

```bash
wget -q "https://download.opensuse.org/opensuse-tdf/15.6/daily/x86_64/OpenSUSE-TDF-15.6-x86_64.iso" -O leap-15.6-tdf.iso
```

---

## Passo 2 – Copiar a ISO para o hostA

Envie a ISO para `hostA`. Troque usuário/permissões conforme o SSH do hostA:

```bash
# De hostX para hostA
sudo scp leap-15.6-cde.iso root@hostA:/opt/openSUSE/iso/

ls -lh /opt/openSUSE/iso/
```

---

## Passo 3 – Conferir a ISO no hostA

Monte a ISO somente para testar se ela pode ser lida:

```bash
# No hostA
sudo umask 0022
sudo mkdir -p /mnt/iso-check
sudo mount -o ro /opt/openSUSE/iso/leap-15.6-cde.iso /mnt/iso-check

ls /mnt/iso-check/usr/bin/bash
sudo umount /mnt/iso-check
```

Se esse comando acima falhar (ISO criptografada ou squashfs incompatível), use QEMU para abrir e ler a ISO:

```bash
# Só se precisar do QEMU em hostA
sudo qemu-img convert -O qcow2 \
  /opt/openSUSE/iso/leap-15.6-cde.iso \
  /opt/openSUSE/work/iso.qcow2

sudo qemu-img attach -o node,read_only=1 \
  /opt/openSUSE/work/iso.qcow2 /dev/sda

sudo mount /dev/sda1 /mnt/iso-check
# Depois use o mesmo /mnt/iso-check no Passo 4
sudo umount /dev/sda1
```

> Se `qemu-img` não estiver instalado no hostA, copie RPMs do `hostX`:  
> `sudo rpm -ivh qemu-img-tools qemu-system-x86_64`

---

## Passo 4 – Copiar o conteúdo do ISO para o rootfs de trabalho

Monte novamente a ISO e copie toda a árvore de raiz para `/opt/openSUSE/work`:

```bash
sudo mount -o ro /opt/openSUSE/iso/leap-15.6-cde.iso /mnt/iso-check

# Copia o sistema já instalado da mídia (mais lento, mas completo)
sudo cp -aP /mnt/iso-check /opt/openSUSE/work

# Opção mais rápida se o arquivo for grande e você tiver rsync:
# rsync -aavz --delete /mnt/iso-check/ /opt/openSUSE/work/

sudo umount /mnt/iso-check

ls -R /opt/openSUSE/work/usr/bin | head
```

Isso inclui `/usr`, `/etc`, `/opt`, `/bin`, `/lib`, `/boot`, entre outros. O que **não** está presente são partições temporárias de runtime, como `/var/log`, `/tmp` etc. Vamos criá-las manualmente.

---

## Passo 5 – Criar diretórios voláteis necessários

```bash
sudo mkdir -p /var/log /var/lib /tmp /run /home /opt/tmp
sudo chmod 1755 /var/log
sudo chmod 1777 /tmp
sudo chmod 755 /run
sudo touch /var/log/rotate
```

Esses diretórios evitam falhas iniciais do systemd e de muitos utilitários.

---

## Passo 6 – Criar o Dockerfile

Crie `/opt/openSUSE/work/Dockerfile`:

```dockerfile
FROM scratch
COPY --chown=root:root . /
RUN ln -sf /usr/bin/systemd /init 2>/dev/null || true
RUN ln -sf /usr/bin/systemctl /systemctl 2>/dev/null || true
RUN printf 'Ambiente base do openSUSE Leap criado a partir da mídia.\n' > /etc/motd
```

Explicação:

- `FROM scratch` começa com uma imagem vazia.
- `COPY --chown=root:root . /` coloca todo o conteúdo copiado no Passo 4 como raiz da imagem.
- Os symlinks garantem um `/init` válido para o systemd iniciar.
- O `/etc/motd` apenas mostra uma mensagem amigável.

> Se sua versão do Podman reclamar de `--chown`, rode sem ele:
> ```bash
> podman build -t openSUSEImage -f Dockerfile .
> ```

---

## Passo 7 – Construir a imagem `openSUSEImage`

Entre no diretório criado e construa:

```bash
cd /opt/openSUSE/work
podman build -t openSUSEImage -f Dockerfile .
```

Confira a criação:

```bash
podman image ls
podman inspect openSUSEImage --format '{{.RepoTags}}'
```

---

## Passo 8 – Validar a imagem

Dentro do container:

```bash
# Mostra a identificação do sistema
podman exec -it openSUSEImage bash -c 'cat /etc/os-release | grep NAME'

# Confere comandos disponíveis
podman exec -it openSUSEImage bash -c 'which rpm systemd bash zypper 2>/dev/null || true'

# Testa um shell interativo
podman run --rm -it openSUSEImage bash
```

Se quiser usar rede, use `--network=host` ou mapeie portas:

```bash
# Compartilha rede com o host (mais exposição)
podman run --rm -it --network=host openSUSEImage bash

# Rede isolada com portas abertas
podman run --rm -it -p 22:22 -p 80:80 --network=bridge openSUSEImage bash
```

---

## Passo 9 – Salvar ou empurrar a imagem

```bash
# Gera um tarball local
podman save -o openSUSEImage.tar openSUSEImage

# Importa em outra máquina
podman image import - openSUSEImage2

# Empurra para um registry privado
podman push openSUSEImage:5000:opensuse
```

---

## Passo 10 – Adicionar pacotes offline extras (opcional)

Se o `hostX` tiver RPMs baixados de reposições offline, copie para o hostA e embuta na imagem.

### 10.1 – Copiar RPMs

```bash
sudo mkdir -p /opt/openSUSE/pkgs
sudo cp /caminho/dos/rpms/. /opt/openSUSE/pkgs/
```

### 10.2 – Criar script de instalação offline

Crie `/opt/openSUSE/scripts/install-offline.sh`:

```bash
#!/bin/bash
PKGDIR="/opt/openSUSE/pkgs"

if [ ! -d "$PKGDIR" ] || [ "$(ls -A "$PKGDIR")" = "" ]; then
    echo "Nenhum RPM encontrado em $PKGDIR"
    exit 1
fi

# Verifica dependências
rpm -Tqp "$PKGDIR"/*.rpm >/dev/null 2>&1 || {
    echo "Erro: alguma dependencia nao foi resolvida."
    exit 1
}

# Instala os RPMs
rpm -ivh --nofork --quiet --nopackage-locking "$PKGDIR"/*.rpm

echo "Pacotes adicionais instalados."
```

Dê execução e adicione ao Dockerfile, antes do `COPY` final:

```dockerfile
RUN bash /opt/openSUSE/scripts/install-offline.sh
```

⚠️ Isso só funciona se **todas as dependências** dos RPMs também estiverem embutidas na imagem. Caso contrário, a instalação para com erro.

---

## Alternativa para uma instalação completamente nova via QEMU

Se você quiser instalar o Leap do zero dentro de uma VM e depois gerar a imagem OCI, o caminho é QEMU + instalador desassistido (`unattended installer`). Resumo:

1. No hostX, baixe a ISO e copie para hostA.
2. No hostA, crie um disco vazio:

```bash
sudo qemu-img fill -f qcow2 -O node -d 50G /opt/openSUSE/work/leap-disk.qcow2
```

3. Monte a ISO como disco de leitura:

Essa imagem serve para rodar o sistema dentro de um container. Ela não é uma instalação interativa ponta a ponta, mas reproduz o sistema já instalado na mídia — útil como base containerizada.

> **Resumo do fluxo:**  
> 1. `hostX` baixa a ISO.  
> 2. ISO é copiada para `hostA`.  
> 3. O conteúdo da ISO é copiado para uma pasta de trabalho.  
> 4. Crio um `Dockerfile`.  
> 5. Rodo `podman build -t openSUSEImage`.  
> 6. Uso a imagem no Podman.

---

## Pré-requisitos

- **hostA:** RHEL 9.2, sem internet, com `podman` ≥ 4.0, `sudo`, pelo menos ~20 GB livres.

## Passo 1 – Baixar a ISO no hostX

Em `hostX`, crie uma pasta e baixe a ISO:

```bash

cd /opt/opensuse-downloads

# Exemplo Leap 15.6 CDE (altere a URL/versão se necessário)
wget -q \
  "https://download.opensuse.org/opensuse-leap/15.6/dvd/live/x86_64/OpenSUSE-Leap-15.6-x86_64-CDE_DVD_20240425.iso" \
  -O leap-15.6-cde.iso

ls -lh leap-15.6-cde.iso
```

Se quiser uma versão mais leve, use o **TDF** (Test Desktop Framework):

```bash

```

---

## Passo 2 – Copiar a ISO para o hostA

Envie a ISO para `hostA`. Troque usuário/permissões conforme o SSH do hostA:

```bash

ls -lh /opt/openSUSE/iso/
```

sudo mkdir -p /mnt/iso-check
sudo mount -o ro /opt/openSUSE/iso/leap-15.6-cde.iso /mnt/iso-check

ls /mnt/iso-check/usr/bin/bash
sudo umount /mnt/iso-check
```

```bash

  /opt/openSUSE/iso/leap-15.6-cde.iso \
  /opt/openSUSE/work/iso.qcow2

sudo qemu-img attach -o node,read_only=1 \
  /opt/openSUSE/work/iso.qcow2 /dev/sda

# Depois use o mesmo /mnt/iso-check no Passo 4
sudo umount /dev/sda1
```

## Passo 4 – Copiar o conteúdo do ISO para o rootfs de trabalho

Monte novamente a ISO e copie toda a árvore de raiz para `/opt/openSUSE/work`:

```bash

# Copia o sistema já instalado da mídia (mais lento, mas completo)

# Opção mais rápida se o arquivo for grande e você tiver rsync:

```

Isso inclui `/usr`, `/etc`, `/opt`, `/bin`, `/lib`, `/boot`, entre outros. O que **não** está presente são partições temporárias de runtime, como `/var/log`, `/tmp` etc. Vamos criá-las manualmente.

```bash

```

Esses diretórios evitam falhas iniciais do systemd e de muitos utilitários.

Crie `/opt/openSUSE/work/Dockerfile`:

```dockerfile
FROM scratch
COPY --chown=root:root . /
RUN ln -sf /usr/bin/systemd /init 2>/dev/null || true
RUN ln -sf /usr/bin/systemctl /systemctl 2>/dev/null || true
RUN printf 'Ambiente base do openSUSE Leap criado a partir da mídia.\n' > /etc/motd
```

- `FROM scratch` começa com uma imagem vazia.
- `COPY --chown=root:root . /` coloca todo o conteúdo copiado no Passo 4 como raiz da imagem.

```bash

Dentro do container:

```bash

podman exec -it openSUSEImage bash -c 'which rpm systemd bash zypper 2>/dev/null || true'

# Testa um shell interativo
podman run --rm -it openSUSEImage bash
```

Se quiser usar rede, use `--network=host` ou mapeie portas:

```bash

podman run --rm -it --network=host openSUSEImage bash

# Rede isolada com portas abertas
podman run --rm -it -p 22:22 -p 80:80 --network=bridge openSUSEImage bash
```

---

## Passo 9 – Salvar ou empurrar a imagem

```bash
# Gera um tarball local
podman save -o openSUSEImage.tar openSUSEImage

# Importa em outra máquina
podman image import - openSUSEImage2

# Empurra para um registry privado
podman push openSUSEImage:5000:opensuse
```

---

## Passo 10 – Adicionar pacotes offline extras (opcional)

Se o `hostX` tiver RPMs baixados de reposições offline, copie para o hostA e embuta na imagem.

### 10.1 – Copiar RPMs

```bash

sudo cp /caminho/dos/rpms/. /opt/openSUSE/pkgs/
```

### 10.2 – Criar script de instalação offline

Crie `/opt/openSUSE/scripts/install-offline.sh`:

```bash
#!/bin/bash

if [ ! -d "$PKGDIR" ] || [ "$(ls -A "$PKGDIR")" = "" ]; then
    echo "Nenhum RPM encontrado em $PKGDIR"
    exit 1
fi

# Verifica dependências

    echo "Erro: alguma dependencia nao foi resolvida."
    exit 1
}

# Instala os RPMs

echo "Pacotes adicionais instalados."
```

Dê execução e adicione ao Dockerfile, antes do `COPY` final:

```dockerfile

Yes. The problem is that `SUM(d.size)` sums **every row** produced by the joins. If the same document appears more than once in `documents_assignment` for the same category, it will be joined multiple times and its size will be added more than once.

Quick fix is to deduplicate the size inside the aggregate:

```sql
SELECT
      d1.*,
      COALESCE(GROUP_CONCAT(DISTINCT d2.id), '') AS children,
      COUNT(DISTINCT da.documentId) AS num_documents,   -- distinct docs assigned
      IFNULL(SUM(DISTINCT d.size), 0) AS total_size     -- sum unique doc sizes
FROM document_categories d1
LEFT JOIN document_categories d2 ON (d2.parentId = d1.id)
LEFT JOIN documents_assignment da ON (da.categoryId = d1.id)
LEFT JOIN documents d ON (da.documentId = d.id)
GROUP BY d1;
```

### Notes

- If each assignment row refers to a **different** document, your original `total_size` is probably already correct.
- The bug mainly happens when the **same** `documentId` has multiple rows in `documents_assignment` for the same category.

WITH doc_sizes AS (
      SELECT id,

      GROUP BY id

      COALESCE(GROUP_CONCAT(DISTINCT d2.id), '') AS children,
      COUNT(DISTINCT da.documentId) AS num_documents,

### My answer to the user

The join to child categories can multiply the document rows: each document is repeated once for each matching child category, so `SUM(d.size)` can become too large. Aggregate document sizes separately, before joining the child categories. Since your document count is distinct, the query below also deduplicates repeated assignments of the same document to the same category:

SELECT
    d1.*,
    COALESCE(GROUP_CONCAT(DISTINCT d2.id), '') AS children,
    COALESCE(stats.num_documents, 0) AS num_documents,
    COALESCE(stats.total_size, 0) AS total_size
FROM document_categories d1
LEFT JOIN document_categories d2
    ON d2.parentId = d1.id
LEFT JOIN (
    SELECT
        pairs.categoryId,
        COUNT(*) AS num_documents,
        SUM(pairs.size) AS total_size
    FROM (
        SELECT DISTINCT
            da.categoryId,
            d.id,
            d.size
        FROM documents_assignment da
        JOIN documents d ON d.id = da.documentId
    ) AS pairs
    GROUP BY pairs.categoryId
) AS stats
    ON stats.categoryId = d1.id
GROUP BY d1.id;
```

> **Assumption Note:** This outline assumes that “V5” refers to **ASVS Level V (Organizational Process Excellence)** or the corresponding highest-maturity verification tier in **ASVS Version 5**. If your reference to “V5” actually concerns the 5th top-level control in the traditional ASVS 4.0 numbering — i.e., **T-LG-05 (Input Validation)** — please indicate so that a tailored outline can be produced.

---

# Guide: ASVS Level V – Achieving Organizational Process Excellence in Application Security

## 1. Introduction
### 1.1 Purpose and Scope
- Define Level V as the target for organizations seeking enterprise-wide, continuously improving application security.
- Clarify that Level V extends beyond technical controls (Level IV) to encompass governance, culture, measurement, and systemic integration.
- Provide a practical roadmap for assessing, designing, implementing, and demonstrating Level V conformance.

### 1.2 Background on ASVS Levels
- Recap ASVS Levels 0–IV (Not Applicable, Fundamental, Medium Effort, High Effort, Rigorous Testing).
- Explain the difference between “rigorous project-level testing” (Level IV) and “organization-wide excellence” (Level V).
- Highlight that Level V requires sustained institutionalization, not one-off efforts.

### 1.3 Defining Level V (Organizational Process Excellence)
- Core tenets: continuous improvement, cross-functional accountability, measurable security posture, embedded security in all lifecycle stages.
- Emphasis on governance frameworks, role clarity, automation, culture, and leadership engagement.
- Relation to maturity models (e.g., CMMI, NIST CSF maturity).

### 1.4 Target Readers
- Security architects, program managers, DevSecOps engineers, IT executives, compliance officers, and auditors.
- Any team responsible for defining and driving application security strategy.

### 1.5 Standards Alignment
- Map Level V practices to:
  - NIST Cybersecurity Framework (CSF)
  - ISO/IEC 27001 and ISO/IEC 27034
  - OWASP Top Ten and associated guidelines
  - DevSecOps and Agile security frameworks

---

## 2. Foundational Concepts for Level V
### 2.1 Security Culture and Awareness
#### 2.1.1 Building a Security-First Culture
- Encourage “secure by default” mindset across all levels.
- Integrate security into mission statements, values, and hiring criteria.

#### 2.1.2 Leadership Visibility and Accountability
- Executive sponsors visibly champion security initiatives.
- Security KPIs reported at board meetings and strategic reviews.

#### 2.1.3 Psychological Safety and Blame-Free Reporting
- Incentivize reporting of vulnerabilities without fear of reprisal.
- Establish non-punitive incident response and reward programs for disclosure.

#### 2.1.4 Ongoing Education and Communication
- Multichannel training (in-person, e-learning, microlearning).
- Regular security newsletters, town halls, and quick-reference guides.

### 2.2 Governance and Risk Management
#### 2.2.1 Enterprise Security Policy Framework
- Centralized policies aligned with business objectives.
- Policy coverage for development, deployment, change management, incident response, and third-party use.

#### 2.2.2 Risk-Based Decision Making
- Formal risk assessment process for new features, systems, and suppliers.
- Prioritization based on attack surface, criticality, and historical threat data.

#### 2.2.3 Role Clarity and RACI Matrix
- Define responsibilities for security champions, app owners, platform teams, and incident responders.
- Publish a RACI matrix for key application security activities.

#### 2.2.4 Alignment with Business Objectives
- Tie security outcomes to business KPIs (e.g., time-to-market, user experience, compliance deadlines).
- Secure budget approval for security investments through business-case presentations.

### 2.3 DevSecOps Integration
#### 2.3.1 Automated Security Gates in CI/CD
- Mandatory SAST, DAST, SCA, container scanning, and secrets management checks.
- Fail-closed gates that block deployments until security thresholds are met.

#### 2.3.2 Shift-Left, Shift-Right, Shift-Left Security Practices
- Security involvement from requirements through retirement.
- Runtime monitoring, anomaly detection, and runtime defense.

#### 2.3.3 Security-as-Code and Infrastructure as Code (IaC)
- Enforce security policies via configuration templates and linting rules.
- Use GitOps workflows with security approvals required for environment changes.

### 2.4 Measurement and Continuous Improvement
#### 2.4.1 Security KPIs and Dashboards
- Track metrics such as vulnerability remediation SLAs, test coverage, incident frequency, and attacker simulation results.
- Visual dashboards accessible to engineering and executive leadership.

#### 2.4.2 Unified Logging and Telemetry
- Standardized logging across all components and services.
- Centralized SIEM/SOAR integration for real-time threat detection.

#### 2.4.3 Incident Response and Learning Loops
- Structured post-incident reviews focused on root cause and process improvement.
- Feed findings back into training, threat models, and policy updates.

---

## 3. Key Requirements and Verification Criteria
### 3.1 Mapping Level V to ASVS Top-Level Controls
> *Example conceptual mapping (not exhaustive).*

| ASVS Control | Level V Expectation |
|--------------|---------------------|
| T-LG-16 Threat Modeling | Organizational threat modeling program with templates, cross-team exercises, and regular updates. |
| T-LG-17 Vulnerability Management | Institutionalized vulnerability disclosure, triage, patching SLAs, and executive trend reporting. |
| T-LG-26 Security Awareness | Measurable training completion rates, annual refreshers, and effectiveness surveys. |
| T-LG-32 DevSecOps | Automated security tooling integrated into all pipelines; security metrics tied to team performance. |
| T-LG-21/22 Supply Chain Security | Vendor risk assessments, SBOM management, dependency scanning, and contract security clauses. |
| T-LG-20 Configuration Management | Hardened baselines, infrastructure audits, and change-review security requirements. |

### 3.2 Defining Verification Evidence
#### 3.2.1 Evidence Collection Methods
- Policies, procedures, meeting minutes, RACI matrices, tool configurations, training records, audit reports, dashboards, and incident post-mortems.
- Demonstrations of automated gates and continuous monitoring.

#### 3.2.2 Assessment Checklist
- Self-assessment questionnaire mapped to Level V criteria.
- Managerial review and sign-off.
- Optional third-party audit for external assurance.

#### 3.2.3 Rating Scale
- **Conformant**: Full evidence and effective practice.
- **Partially Conformant**: Partial evidence or ad-hoc implementation.
- **Non-Conformant**: No evidence or significant gaps.
- **Not Applicable**: Justified exemption documented.

---

## 4. Implementation Strategy
### 4.1 Phase 1: Diagnostic and Baseline Establishment
#### 4.1.1 Current State Assessment
- Security posture scan across environments.
- Interviews with development, DevOps, QA, and operations teams.
- Review of existing policies, tooling, and incident history.

#### 4.1.2 Gap Analysis
- Compare current practices against Level V requirements.
- Prioritize gaps by risk severity, effort, and business impact.

### 4.2 Phase 2: Governance and Process Design
#### 4.2.1 Establish Security Champions/Advocates
- Train representatives per team to act as local security liaisons.
- Rotate champions periodically to broaden expertise.

#### 4.2.2 Policy and Procedure Updates
- Draft/update security policies covering dev, deploy, ops, incident response, and third parties.
- Ensure policies are concise, actionable, and reviewed quarterly.

#### 4.2.3 Define Change Management Security Gates
- Require security review for production-impacting changes.
- Integrate approval workflows into change management systems.

#### 4.2.4 Executive and Board Engagement
- Produce monthly/unmonthly security scorecards.
- Schedule board-level briefings on critical risks and mitigations.

### 4.3 Phase 3: Training and Cultural Transformation
#### 4.3.1 Security Awareness Program
- Mandatory initial onboarding security training.
- Annual refresher and micro-learning modules.
- Gamified challenges and phishing simulators.

#### 4.3.2 Role-Specific Curricula
- Developers, QA, DevOps, testers, system admins, and incident responders.
- Curriculum focuses on applicable tasks (e.g., secure code review, pipeline security, log hygiene).

#### 4.3.3 Incentives and Recognition
- Award security hackathons, “Bug Bounty” recognition.
- Link security KPIs to team bonuses or career development where appropriate.

### 4.4 Phase 4: Automation and Tooling Investment
#### 4.4.1 Centralized Security Testing Platforms
- Integrate SAST, DAST, SCA, infrastructure scanning, and secret leakage detection.
- Results feed into ticketing and CI/CD dashboards.

#### 4.4.2 Infrastructure Security
- Scan IaC files (TF, Kubernetes manifests, Dockerfiles) for compliance.
- Enforce baselines via Helm charts, Ansible inventories, or Terraform modules.

#### 4.4.3 Secrets and Credentials Management
- Use vault solutions (HashiCorp Vault, AWS Secrets Manager) with auto-rotation.
- Enforce least-privilege access to secrets.

#### 4.4.4 Security Policy Enforcement
- Implement policy-as-code for CI/CD gates (e.g.,OPA, Checkov).
- Block merges/deployments that violate security rules.

### 4.5 Phase 5: Measurement and Continuous Improvement
#### 4.5.1 KPI Dashboard Design
- Track remediation times, vulnerability trends, incident rates, and training completion.
- Segment by team, service, or environment.

#### 4.5.2 Quarterly Security Reviews
- Present findings, discuss root causes, assign owners, and review progress.
- Document decisions and corrective actions in a living repository.

#### 4.5.3 Red Teaming and Adversarial Simulations
- Conduct annual or biannual red-team exercises targeting critical attack paths.
- Use insights to refine defenses and security controls.

#### 4.5.4 Lessons Learned Repository
- Maintain a database of past incidents, vulnerability classes, and effective mitigations.
- Update training content and threat models based on this data.

### 4.6 Phase 6: Scaling and Enterprise-Wide Maturity
#### 4.6.1 Multi-Team and Geographic Expansion
- Roll out standardized practices across all engineering and operations sites.
- Use security champions network to coordinate globally.

#### 4.6.2 Performance Management Integration
- Incorporate security metrics into team OKRs where feasible.
- Recognize teams that consistently meet security goals.

#### 4.6.3 Innovation Hub for Security Automation
- Dedicate resources to experiment with emerging security technologies (e.g., AI-driven threat detection, zero-trust architectures).
- Pilot innovations and scale successful ones.

#### 4.6.4 External Benchmarking
- Compare results against industry benchmarks (CIS Controls, Cloud Security Blueprint, MITRE ATO).
- Pursue certifications that reflect Level V maturity (e.g., ISO 27001).

---

## 5. Best Practices
### 5.1 Embed Security Early and Everywhere
- Include security requirements in backlog grooming and agile ceremonies.
- Provide security templates for API design, cloud infrastructure, and microservices.

### 5.2 Foster Cross-Functional Collaboration
- Break down silos through joint sprints, shared dashboards, and unified incident teams.
- Create DevSecOps roles with equal authority over tech and security decisions.

### 5.3 Automate Where Possible, Judge Where Needed
- Use automation for repetitive checks (scanning, compliance).
- Retain human experts for complex risk assessments and exception handling.

### 5.4 Adopt a Risk-Based Approach
- Allocate security resources based on asset criticality, exposure, and historical threats.
- Do not apply identical controls to low-risk and high-risk services.

### 5.5 Keep Documentation Living
- Use templated documents and version control.
- Review and update policies, threat models, and runbooks quarterly or after significant events.

### 5.6 Manage Third-Party Risk Systematically
- Require security questionnaires, SBOMs, and contract clauses for all external integrations.
- Continuously monitor vendor security postures via scorecards and vulnerability feeds.

### 5.7 Leverage Real-Time Threat Intelligence
- Integrate threat feeds into SOC and CI/CD pipelines.
- Use indicators of compromise (IoCs) to automate blocking and alerting.

### 5.8 Cultivate Transparency and Openness
- Publish internal vulnerability advisories and mitigation plans.
- Encourage communities (internal and external) to contribute security ideas and patches.

---

## 6. Common Challenges and Mitigation Strategies
### 6.1 Lack of Executive Sponsorship
- Build compelling business cases showing cost avoidance and business continuity benefits.
- Report directly to the C-suite with clear risk narratives.

### 6.2 Resource Constraints
- Start with high-risk services and automate lower-effort tasks.
- Prioritize investment in reusable tooling over one-off fixes.

### 6.3 Team Resistance to Change
- Involve teams early in process design.
- Provide clear benefits (e.g., reduced firefighting, clearer roles, faster incident resolution).
- Use peer champions to influence skeptics.

### 6.4 Overly Manual Processes
- Set concrete automation targets (e.g., 80% of security checks automated within 12 months).
- Invest in scripting, CI/CD gates, and policy-as-code.

### 6.5 Inconsistent Metrics
- Standardize metric definitions and data sources across the organization.
- Use a single consolidated dashboard for consistency.

### 6.6 Third-Party Non-Compliance
- Enforce security requirements in master service agreements.
- Require evidence of compliance for critical vendors.

### 6.7 Knowledge Loss and Turnover
- Document every role and responsibility.
- Cross-train personnel and rotate security champions to maintain expertise.

---

### 2.1 Validation
- Validate data against expected type, format, length, range, and business rules
- Prefer allowlists for constrained inputs
- Validate on the server, even when client-side checks are also used

### 2.2 Normalization and Canonicalization
- Define when and how inputs are normalized
- Avoid inconsistent handling of encoded or equivalent representations
- Validate at the appropriate point in the normalization process

### 2.3 Sanitization
- Distinguish sanitization from validation and output encoding
- Use sanitization only where the application must accept and transform content, such as permitted rich text
- Prefer well-maintained, context-appropriate libraries over custom filters

### 2.4 Contextual Output Encoding
- Explain why encoding depends on the destination context
- Cover HTML, HTML attributes, JavaScript, URL, CSS, and other relevant contexts
- Avoid unsafe interpolation and double-encoding

## 3. Threats and Failure Modes
- Injection caused by treating data as executable syntax
- Cross-site scripting and unsafe rich-text handling
- Parser and format confusion
- Bypasses caused by inconsistent normalization or validation
- Common mistakes: denylist-only checks, client-side-only validation, and generic “sanitize everything” routines

## 4. Secure Design and Implementation Practices
### 4.1 Input Handling
- Identify and document trust boundaries and input sources
- Apply server-side, allowlist-based validation where feasible
- Enforce limits on size, type, range, and structure
- Handle invalid input safely and consistently

### 4.2 Database and Interpreter Boundaries
- Use parameterized queries or prepared statements for database access
- Use safe APIs for operating-system commands, templates, and other interpreters
- Do not rely on escaping or encoding as a replacement for structured APIs

### 4.3 Output and Content Handling
- Use framework-provided contextual output encoding
- Sanitize user-authored HTML with a maintained allowlist-based HTML sanitizer when HTML is required
- Set safe content types and avoid unsafe DOM APIs where applicable

### 4.4 File and Structured Data Inputs
- Validate file type, size, and structure; do not trust file extensions or client-provided MIME types alone
- Use safe parsers and impose resource limits
- Validate JSON, XML, and other structured data against expected schemas or rules

- Threat-model input and output paths during design
- Provide shared validation and encoding patterns or libraries for development teams
- Add code review guidance for interpreter and browser boundaries
- Integrate static and dynamic analysis, fuzzing, and security tests into CI/CD
- Reassess controls when frameworks, parsers, or input sources change

- Map applicable V5 requirements to application features and data flows
- Test both valid and invalid inputs, including boundary cases and alternate encodings
- Verify context-specific encoding in rendered output
- Test that database and command interfaces use safe structured APIs
- Record evidence, exceptions, and remediation decisions

- Monitor relevant failures and abuse patterns without logging sensitive data unnecessarily
- Keep sanitization, parsing, and framework dependencies updated
- Review validation rules as business requirements evolve

# Guide: ASVS Level V – Achieving Organizational Process Excellence in Application Security

## 1. Introduction
### 1.1 Purpose and Scope
- Define Level V as the target for organizations seeking enterprise-wide, continuously improving application security.
- Clarify that Level V extends beyond technical controls (Level IV) to encompass governance, culture, measurement, and systemic integration.
- Provide a practical roadmap for assessing, designing, implementing, and demonstrating Level V conformance.

### 1.2 Background on ASVS Levels
- Recap ASVS Levels 0–IV (Not Applicable, Fundamental, Medium Effort, High Effort, Rigorous Testing).
- Explain the difference between “rigorous project-level testing” (Level IV) and “organization-wide excellence” (Level V).
- Highlight that Level V requires sustained institutionalization, not one-off efforts.

### 1.3 Defining Level V (Organizational Process Excellence)
- Core tenets: continuous improvement, cross-functional accountability, measurable security posture, embedded security in all lifecycle stages.
- Emphasis on governance frameworks, role clarity, automation, culture, and leadership engagement.
- Relation to maturity models (e.g., CMMI, NIST CSF maturity).

### 1.4 Target Readers
- Security architects, program managers, DevSecOps engineers, IT executives, compliance officers, and auditors.
- Any team responsible for defining and driving application security strategy.

### 1.5 Standards Alignment
- Map Level V practices to:
  - NIST Cybersecurity Framework (CSF)
  - ISO/IEC 27001 and ISO/IEC 27034
  - OWASP Top Ten and associated guidelines
  - DevSecOps and Agile security frameworks

---

## 2. Foundational Concepts for Level V
### 2.1 Security Culture and Awareness
#### 2.1.1 Building a Security-First Culture
- Encourage “secure by default” mindset across all levels.
- Integrate security into mission statements, values, and hiring criteria.

#### 2.1.2 Leadership Visibility and Accountability
- Executive sponsors visibly champion security initiatives.
- Security KPIs reported at board meetings and strategic reviews.

#### 2.1.3 Psychological Safety and Blame-Free Reporting
- Incentivize reporting of vulnerabilities without fear of reprisal.
- Establish non-punitive incident response and reward programs for disclosure.

#### 2.1.4 Ongoing Education and Communication
- Multichannel training (in-person, e-learning, microlearning).
- Regular security newsletters, town halls, and quick-reference guides.

### 2.2 Governance and Risk Management
#### 2.2.1 Enterprise Security Policy Framework
- Centralized policies aligned with business objectives.
- Policy coverage for development, deployment, change management, incident response, and third-party use.

#### 2.2.2 Risk-Based Decision Making
- Formal risk assessment process for new features, systems, and suppliers.
- Prioritization based on attack surface, criticality, and historical threat data.

#### 2.2.3 Role Clarity and RACI Matrix
- Define responsibilities for security champions, app owners, platform teams, and incident responders.
- Publish a RACI matrix for key application security activities.

#### 2.2.4 Alignment with Business Objectives
- Tie security outcomes to business KPIs (e.g., time-to-market, user experience, compliance deadlines).
- Secure budget approval for security investments through business-case presentations.

### 2.3 DevSecOps Integration
#### 2.3.1 Automated Security Gates in CI/CD
- Mandatory SAST, DAST, SCA, container scanning, and secrets management checks.
- Fail-closed gates that block deployments until security thresholds are met.

#### 2.3.2 Shift-Left, Shift-Right, Shift-Left Security Practices
- Security involvement from requirements through retirement.
- Runtime monitoring, anomaly detection, and runtime defense.

#### 2.3.3 Security-as-Code and Infrastructure as Code (IaC)
- Enforce security policies via configuration templates and linting rules.
- Use GitOps workflows with security approvals required for environment changes.

### 2.4 Measurement and Continuous Improvement
#### 2.4.1 Security KPIs and Dashboards
- Track metrics such as vulnerability remediation SLAs, test coverage, incident frequency, and attacker simulation results.
- Visual dashboards accessible to engineering and executive leadership.

#### 2.4.2 Unified Logging and Telemetry
- Standardized logging across all components and services.
- Centralized SIEM/SOAR integration for real-time threat detection.

#### 2.4.3 Incident Response and Learning Loops
- Structured post-incident reviews focused on root cause and process improvement.
- Feed findings back into training, threat models, and policy updates.

---

## 3. Key Requirements and Verification Criteria
### 3.1 Mapping Level V to ASVS Top-Level Controls
> *Example conceptual mapping (not exhaustive).*

| ASVS Control | Level V Expectation |
|--------------|---------------------|
| T-LG-16 Threat Modeling | Organizational threat modeling program with templates, cross-team exercises, and regular updates. |
| T-LG-17 Vulnerability Management | Institutionalized vulnerability disclosure, triage, patching SLAs, and executive trend reporting. |
| T-LG-26 Security Awareness | Measurable training completion rates, annual refreshers, and effectiveness surveys. |
| T-LG-32 DevSecOps | Automated security tooling integrated into all pipelines; security metrics tied to team performance. |
| T-LG-21/22 Supply Chain Security | Vendor risk assessments, SBOM management, dependency scanning, and contract security clauses. |
| T-LG-20 Configuration Management | Hardened baselines, infrastructure audits, and change-review security requirements. |

### 3.2 Defining Verification Evidence
#### 3.2.1 Evidence Collection Methods
- Policies, procedures, meeting minutes, RACI matrices, tool configurations, training records, audit reports, dashboards, and incident post-mortems.
- Demonstrations of automated gates and continuous monitoring.

#### 3.2.2 Assessment Checklist
- Self-assessment questionnaire mapped to Level V criteria.
- Managerial review and sign-off.
- Optional third-party audit for external assurance.

#### 3.2.3 Rating Scale
- **Conformant**: Full evidence and effective practice.
- **Partially Conformant**: Partial evidence or ad-hoc implementation.
- **Non-Conformant**: No evidence or significant gaps.
- **Not Applicable**: Justified exemption documented.

---

## 4. Implementation Strategy
### 4.1 Phase 1: Diagnostic and Baseline Establishment
#### 4.1.1 Current State Assessment
- Security posture scan across environments.
- Interviews with development, DevOps, QA, and operations teams.
- Review of existing policies, tooling, and incident history.

#### 4.1.2 Gap Analysis
- Compare current practices against Level V requirements.
- Prioritize gaps by risk severity, effort, and business impact.

### 4.2 Phase 2: Governance and Process Design
#### 4.2.1 Establish Security Champions/Advocates
- Train representatives per team to act as local security liaisons.
- Rotate champions periodically to broaden expertise.

#### 4.2.2 Policy and Procedure Updates
- Draft/update security policies covering dev, deploy, ops, incident response, and third parties.
- Ensure policies are concise, actionable, and reviewed quarterly.

#### 4.2.3 Define Change Management Security Gates
- Require security review for production-impacting changes.
- Integrate approval workflows into change management systems.

#### 4.2.4 Executive and Board Engagement
- Produce monthly/unmonthly security scorecards.
- Schedule board-level briefings on critical risks and mitigations.

### 4.3 Phase 3: Training and Cultural Transformation
#### 4.3.1 Security Awareness Program
- Mandatory initial onboarding security training.
- Annual refresher and micro-learning modules.
- Gamified challenges and phishing simulators.

#### 4.3.2 Role-Specific Curricula
- Developers, QA, DevOps, testers, system admins, and incident responders.
- Curriculum focuses on applicable tasks (e.g., secure code review, pipeline security, log hygiene).

#### 4.3.3 Incentives and Recognition
- Award security hackathons, “Bug Bounty” recognition.
- Link security KPIs to team bonuses or career development where appropriate.

### 4.4 Phase 4: Automation and Tooling Investment
#### 4.4.1 Centralized Security Testing Platforms
- Integrate SAST, DAST, SCA, infrastructure scanning, and secret leakage detection.
- Results feed into ticketing and CI/CD dashboards.

#### 4.4.2 Infrastructure Security
- Scan IaC files (TF, Kubernetes manifests, Dockerfiles) for compliance.
- Enforce baselines via Helm charts, Ansible inventories, or Terraform modules.

#### 4.4.3 Secrets and Credentials Management
- Use vault solutions (HashiCorp Vault, AWS Secrets Manager) with auto-rotation.
- Enforce least-privilege access to secrets.

#### 4.4.4 Security Policy Enforcement
- Implement policy-as-code for CI/CD gates (e.g.,OPA, Checkov).
- Block merges/deployments that violate security rules.

### 4.5 Phase 5: Measurement and Continuous Improvement
#### 4.5.1 KPI Dashboard Design
- Track remediation times, vulnerability trends, incident rates, and training completion.
- Segment by team, service, or environment.

#### 4.5.2 Quarterly Security Reviews
- Present findings, discuss root causes, assign owners, and review progress.
- Document decisions and corrective actions in a living repository.

#### 4.5.3 Red Teaming and Adversarial Simulations
- Conduct annual or biannual red-team exercises targeting critical attack paths.
- Use insights to refine defenses and security controls.

#### 4.5.4 Lessons Learned Repository
- Maintain a database of past incidents, vulnerability classes, and effective mitigations.
- Update training content and threat models based on this data.

### 4.6 Phase 6: Scaling and Enterprise-Wide Maturity
#### 4.6.1 Multi-Team and Geographic Expansion
- Roll out standardized practices across all engineering and operations sites.
- Use security champions network to coordinate globally.

#### 4.6.2 Performance Management Integration
- Incorporate security metrics into team OKRs where feasible.
- Recognize teams that consistently meet security goals.

#### 4.6.3 Innovation Hub for Security Automation
- Dedicate resources to experiment with emerging security technologies (e.g., AI-driven threat detection, zero-trust architectures).
- Pilot innovations and scale successful ones.

#### 4.6.4 External Benchmarking
- Compare results against industry benchmarks (CIS Controls, Cloud Security Blueprint, MITRE ATO).
- Pursue certifications that reflect Level V maturity (e.g., ISO 27001).

---

## 5. Best Practices
### 5.1 Embed Security Early and Everywhere
- Include security requirements in backlog grooming and agile ceremonies.
- Provide security templates for API design, cloud infrastructure, and microservices.

### 5.2 Foster Cross-Functional Collaboration
- Break down silos through joint sprints, shared dashboards, and unified incident teams.
- Create DevSecOps roles with equal authority over tech and security decisions.

### 5.3 Automate Where Possible, Judge Where Needed
- Use automation for repetitive checks (scanning, compliance).
- Retain human experts for complex risk assessments and exception handling.

### 5.4 Adopt a Risk-Based Approach
- Allocate security resources based on asset criticality, exposure, and historical threats.
- Do not apply identical controls to low-risk and high-risk services.

### 5.5 Keep Documentation Living
- Use templated documents and version control.
- Review and update policies, threat models, and runbooks quarterly or after significant events.

### 5.6 Manage Third-Party Risk Systematically
- Require security questionnaires, SBOMs, and contract clauses for all external integrations.
- Continuously monitor vendor security postures via scorecards and vulnerability feeds.

### 5.7 Leverage Real-Time Threat Intelligence
- Integrate threat feeds into SOC and CI/CD pipelines.
- Use indicators of compromise (IoCs) to automate blocking and alerting.

### 5.8 Cultivate Transparency and Openness
- Publish internal vulnerability advisories and mitigation plans.
- Encourage communities (internal and external) to contribute security ideas and patches.

---

## 6. Common Challenges and Mitigation Strategies
### 6.1 Lack of Executive Sponsorship
- Build compelling business cases showing cost avoidance and business continuity benefits.
- Report directly to the C-suite with clear risk narratives.

### 6.2 Resource Constraints
- Start with high-risk services and automate lower-effort tasks.
- Prioritize investment in reusable tooling over one-off fixes.

### 6.3 Team Resistance to Change
- Involve teams early in process design.
- Provide clear benefits (e.g., reduced firefighting, clearer roles, faster incident resolution).
- Use peer champions to influence skeptics.

### 6.4 Overly Manual Processes
- Set concrete automation targets (e.g., 80% of security checks automated within 12 months).
- Invest in scripting, CI/CD gates, and policy-as-code.

### 6.5 Inconsistent Metrics
- Standardize metric definitions and data sources across the organization.
- Use a single consolidated dashboard for consistency.

### 6.6 Third-Party Non-Compliance
- Enforce security requirements in master service agreements.
- Require evidence of compliance for critical vendors.

### 6.7 Knowledge Loss and Turnover
- Document every role and responsibility.
- Cross-train personnel and rotate security champions to maintain expertise.

---

## 7. Evaluation and Demonstration of Conformance
### 7.1 Internal Audit Process
- Use a Level V-specific checklist to self-audit.
- Obtain managerial sign-off on evidence packages.

### 7.2 Third-Party Assurance Activities
- Engage independent auditors to review evidence and assess maturity.
- Prepare for certification exams or regulatory inquiries.

### 7.3 Evidence Pack Contents

# Guide Outline: OWASP ASVS V5 — Validation, Sanitization, and Encoding

## 1. Introduction
- Explain V5’s purpose and scope within the ASVS.
- Clarify that V5 concerns safe handling of data—not an ASVS “Level V.”
- Describe how its practices help prevent injection and unsafe content handling.

## 2. Core Concepts
### 2.1 Trust Boundaries and Data Flows
- Identify inputs from users, APIs, files, databases, and third-party services.
- Track data from entry through processing, storage, and output.

### 2.2 Validation
- Check data against expected type, format, length, range, and business rules.
- Prefer allowlists and server-side validation; treat client-side checks as usability features only.

### 2.3 Normalization and Canonicalization
- Normalize data consistently before validating it.
- Avoid inconsistent decoding or repeated normalization that can enable bypasses.

### 2.4 Sanitization
- Define when transformation is appropriate, such as permitting a restricted subset of rich text.
- Avoid treating generic “cleaning” as a substitute for validation, safe APIs, or output encoding.

### 2.5 Contextual Output Encoding
- Encode data for its destination context, such as HTML text, HTML attributes, JavaScript, CSS, or URLs.
- Prefer framework-provided safe templating and escaping.

## 3. Implementation Practices
### 3.1 Input Validation
- Validate at server-side trust boundaries.
- Apply schema, type, length, range, and domain-specific checks.
- Validate structured inputs, including API payloads and file metadata.

### 3.2 Preventing Injection
- Use parameterized queries or safe query builders for database access.
- Use safe APIs and argument separation for operating-system commands.
- Do not rely on escaping or validation alone to make dynamically constructed queries or commands safe.

### 3.3 Output Handling
- Encode at the point of output using the correct context.
- Avoid double encoding and unsafe bypasses of framework escaping.
- Apply content security controls as defense in depth, not as replacements for encoding.

### 3.4 Files and Special Input Types
- Validate file size, type, content, and storage location.
- Handle encodings, archives, and structured formats defensively.
- Restrict accepted values for headers, URLs, and other sensitive sinks.

## 4. Development and Deployment Strategy
- Add V5 requirements to design reviews and threat modeling.
- Provide secure coding patterns and reusable validation/encoding libraries.
- Integrate static analysis, dynamic testing, fuzzing, and code review into CI/CD.
- Monitor and update controls as frameworks and threats evolve.

## 5. Verification and Evidence
- Review data flows and identify trust boundaries and output contexts.
- Test validation rules, normalization behavior, and injection resistance.
- Verify safe API use, template escaping, and file-handling controls.
- Document exceptions, test results, and remediation.

## 6. Common Pitfalls
- Relying only on client-side validation.
- Using blocklists or generic sanitizers as a universal defense.
- Confusing SQL parameterization with output encoding.
- Validating before inconsistent decoding or normalization.
- Logging sensitive input or returning overly detailed errors.

## 7. Practical Resources
- Include checklists, test cases, language-specific examples, and links to relevant OWASP guidance.
- Provide a V5 implementation and verification checklist for development teams.

- Highlight that Level V requires sustained institutionalization, not one-off efforts.

### 1.3 Defining Level V (Organizational Process Excellence)
- Core tenets: continuous improvement, cross-functional accountability, measurable security posture, embedded security in all lifecycle stages.
- Emphasis on governance frameworks, role clarity, automation, culture, and leadership engagement.
- Relation to maturity models (e.g., CMMI, NIST CSF maturity).

- Security architects, program managers, DevSecOps engineers, IT executives, compliance officers, and auditors.

### 1.5 Standards Alignment

  - NIST Cybersecurity Framework (CSF)

---

## 2. Foundational Concepts for Level V
### 2.1 Security Culture and Awareness
#### 2.1.1 Building a Security-First Culture
- Encourage “secure by default” mindset across all levels.
- Integrate security into mission statements, values, and hiring criteria.

#### 2.1.2 Leadership Visibility and Accountability
- Executive sponsors visibly champion security initiatives.
- Security KPIs reported at board meetings and strategic reviews.

#### 2.1.3 Psychological Safety and Blame-Free Reporting
- Incentivize reporting of vulnerabilities without fear of reprisal.
- Establish non-punitive incident response and reward programs for disclosure.

#### 2.1.4 Ongoing Education and Communication
- Multichannel training (in-person, e-learning, microlearning).

### 2.2 Governance and Risk Management
#### 2.2.1 Enterprise Security Policy Framework
- Centralized policies aligned with business objectives.
- Policy coverage for development, deployment, change management, incident response, and third-party use.

#### 2.2.2 Risk-Based Decision Making
- Formal risk assessment process for new features, systems, and suppliers.
- Prioritization based on attack surface, criticality, and historical threat data.

#### 2.2.3 Role Clarity and RACI Matrix
- Define responsibilities for security champions, app owners, platform teams, and incident responders.
- Publish a RACI matrix for key application security activities.

#### 2.2.4 Alignment with Business Objectives
- Tie security outcomes to business KPIs (e.g., time-to-market, user experience, compliance deadlines).

#### 2.3.1 Automated Security Gates in CI/CD
- Mandatory SAST, DAST, SCA, container scanning, and secrets management checks.

#### 2.3.2 Shift-Left, Shift-Right, Shift-Left Security Practices
- Security involvement from requirements through retirement.
- Runtime monitoring, anomaly detection, and runtime defense.

#### 2.3.3 Security-as-Code and Infrastructure as Code (IaC)
- Enforce security policies via configuration templates and linting rules.
- Use GitOps workflows with security approvals required for environment changes.

### 2.4 Measurement and Continuous Improvement
#### 2.4.1 Security KPIs and Dashboards
- Track metrics such as vulnerability remediation SLAs, test coverage, incident frequency, and attacker simulation results.
- Visual dashboards accessible to engineering and executive leadership.

#### 2.4.2 Unified Logging and Telemetry
- Standardized logging across all components and services.
- Centralized SIEM/SOAR integration for real-time threat detection.

- Structured post-incident reviews focused on root cause and process improvement.

- Conduct annual or biannual red-team exercises targeting critical attack paths.
- Use insights to refine defenses and security controls.

- Maintain a database of past incidents, vulnerability classes, and effective mitigations.
- Update training content and threat models based on this data.

- Roll out standardized practices across all engineering and operations sites.
- Use security champions network to coordinate globally.

- Incorporate security metrics into team OKRs where feasible.
- Recognize teams that consistently meet security goals.

#### 4.6.3 Innovation Hub for Security Automation
- Dedicate resources to experiment with emerging security technologies (e.g., AI-driven threat detection, zero-trust architectures).

- Compare results against industry benchmarks (CIS Controls, Cloud Security Blueprint, MITRE ATO).
